newsitem.title: USA: US municipal bond issuers seek repeal of rule.
newsitem.headline: US municipal bond issuers seek repeal of rule.

text.p: Twenty-two state and local government groups blanketed the U.S. House of Representatives on Wednesday with letters opposing repeal of the two-percent "de minimis" rule on corporate holdings of tax-exempt bonds.

Groups representing city and county officials, port authorities, airports, public power agencies, colleges, school boards and others asked House members to sign a letter that U.S. Rep. Phil English, R-Pa., is circulating to House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, R-Texas, opposing repeal.
Currently, the Internal Revenue Service does not permit taxpayers to deduct interest payments on the debt they take on when they purchase tax-exempt bonds.

But the Internal Revenue Service said in 1972, in what is dubbed the de minimis rule, that it will not monitor whether a corporation has borrowed to purchase tax-exempt bonds as long as those holdings total less than two percent of a firm's net assets.
President Clinton in his proposed fiscal 1998 federal budget called for repeal of a series of corporate tax "loopholes" in the U.S. tax code, including the de minimis rule.

Wednesday's letter comes one week after Archer's panel held a hearing on Clinton's repeal proposals. Arthur Hyde, chairman of the corporate bond division of the PSA, testified that Clinton's plan "would make it more expensive for state and local governments to finance vital public services."

The state and local groups on Wednesday warned that de minimis repeal not only would raise the costs of tax-exempt borrowing and leasing for localities, but it would hamper financing of infrastructure and other capital facilities.

The groups, spearheaded by the Government Finance Officers Association, said localities lease various types of equipment, including schools, school buses, software, telecommunications systems, prisons, computers, medical equipment, courthouses and energy management systems.
Without the de minimis rule, "government lessees will face a 41 percent increase in their borrowing rate," the groups said.
